scope: How an end-to-end (E2E) spec is written so it tests what a user does and stays stable: the locators it uses (role, label, text, test id) and those it avoids, how it waits without fixed sleeps and keeps each test's state isolated, when it mocks the network (hermetic) and when it runs against a live or preview environment and how the two are kept apart, how it gets test accounts and secrets without committing them, and how it states the rationale for what it asserts. That E2E runs at all and which journeys it covers (testing/the-testing-workflow), the TypeScript tool choice (implementing/testing/testing), how many E2E tests a suite holds (planning/testing/test-pyramid), contracts (testing/contract-testing), preview environments (shipping/ephemeral-environments), flaky-test quarantine (testing/flaky-test-quarantine) and failure triage (test-failure-triage) are other topics' and are not researched here.
research_type: Technology / software (intent Do; domain browser and mobile end-to-end UI testing; Technical MEDIUM bar: official current docs, recency; no escalation)

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient (browser and mobile E2E UI testing, a technical domain), go first to the tool and platform owners' own documentation (Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO, Selenium, Testing Library, W3C WAI-ARIA, Apple XCUIAutomation/UIKit, Android Espresso/Compose/UI Automator, Microsoft UI Automation), then to standards and security owners for secrets and test data (OWASP ASVS and Secrets Management Cheat Sheet, GitHub Actions docs, the UK ICO) and the ISTQB Foundation syllabus for traceability; use practitioner sources (martinfowler.com, Kent C. Dodds, Thoughtworks Technology Radar) only for the expert's view and for what no primary covers.
methodology.search_strategy: Direct fetches of the known owner documentation pages (best practices, locators, auth, mock, clock, retries, projects, annotations, parameterize, fixtures; Cypress best practices, network requests, environment variables, cy.session; WebdriverIO selectors and best practices; Selenium locators, waits, shared state, page objects, application state, external services), plus web searches for test-data privacy and test-basis traceability. Apple documentation was read through its JSON documentation endpoint because the HTML pages render client-side.
methodology.inclusion: Owner or standards-body text that bears on locators, waiting, isolation, network mocking versus live runs, tagging and gating, credentials and test data, or the rationale behind assertions; practitioner texts by recognised testing authors for the expert's view.
methodology.exclusion: Team-specific layouts, tags, selectors, mocks, output contracts and registries (owner ruling 2026-11-21); vendor marketing; pages that could not be fetched (their claims are not made).

summary: Four of the five listed rules hold. Deterministic specs (write-deterministic-specs) are what every tool owner asks for: Playwright calls tests that wait for time inherently flaky, and Android, Selenium, WebdriverIO, Cypress and Fowler all reject fixed sleeps in favour of waiting on a condition. Hermetic specs stub the network through the tool's interception API (hermetic-specs-mock-the-api): Playwright tells you to use its Network API rather than servers you do not control, and Cypress recommends stubbing for most tests with a real server kept for the critical paths. Credentials stay out of the repository (no-credentials-or-real-user-data): OWASP ASVS 2.10.4 requires it, and Playwright and Cypress keep secrets in environment variables and git-ignored files. Real user data is kept out by the data-minimisation principle and Thoughtworks' Hold on production data in test environments. Tracing a test to its test basis is SHOULD-strength practice (ISTQB), which supports rationale-cites-assertion-source. No source makes an untraced rationale a fail, so rationale-names-what-makes-assertion-correct is unsupported at that strength. The research adds rules the topic lacks: locators that face the user first (role, label, text) with a test id only when none fits, and no CSS/XPath DOM paths; waiting on conditions, never on time; isolated test state set up programmatically; a controlled clock; retries that report flakiness instead of hiding it; hermetic by default with live runs kept to the critical paths and selected by tag or project; credentials from the environment or CI secrets, stored auth state git-ignored, dedicated test accounts; traces on CI failure; page objects that hold no assertions; and E2E assertions that do not repeat what lower-level tests already cover. Apple, Android and Microsoft UI Automation each publish an identifier for automation (accessibilityIdentifier, test tags or resource ids, AutomationId) and condition-based waits.
open_questions: Whether a rationale that does not cite its feature doc, plan or commit is a fail (MUST, as rationale-names-what-makes-assertion-correct states) or a SHOULD, which is what the ISTQB traceability text supports.

Whether a test id may be a first-choice locator: Playwright calls test ids the most resilient way of testing, while Testing Library recommends them only when no role or text match fits; the owner decides which order the cookbook adopts.

Whether hermetic is the default for every spec, and how many live or preview specs a suite keeps (Cypress suggests one true end-to-end test per feature with the rest stubbed); the count itself belongs to the test-pyramid topic.
How live specs are selected and gated: by tag and grep, by a separate project or directory, or by an environment variable; the sources show all three and prefer none.
Whether CI retries are allowed for E2E specs and how many; Playwright and Android both offer retries and both say a test that passes on retry is flaky and must be fixed.

Whether the rule against real user data in a patch is kept at MUST strength: its credentials half rests on OWASP ASVS, its personal-data half on the data-minimisation principle and a Thoughtworks Hold rather than a test-specific requirement.
Whether page objects are recommended, allowed or left to the team, given that Cypress lists sharing page objects as an anti-pattern while Selenium and Playwright's fixture guide build on them.
limitations: Apple's XCUIAutomation and UIKit pages render client-side; they were read through Apple's JSON documentation endpoint. No Apple text was found on locator priority or on fixed sleeps beyond waitForExistence(timeout:).
The Google Testing Blog posts 'Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests' and 'Hermetic Servers' were fetched but their article bodies did not render, so no claim rests on them.

The UK Ministry of Justice guidance on live data for testing, named by a search result as prohibiting live personal data, returned 404 and is not cited; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B.3.31 was not read (paywalled).
The ISTQB glossary entries for test basis and test oracle were not read; the CTFL v4.0.1 syllabus section 1.4.4 stands in for traceability.
WAI-ARIA 1.2 was read only to its first 100,000 characters (definitions and roles), enough for the claims made.
No published study was found that measures flake rates by locator type or by waiting strategy; the stability claims rest on owner documentation and practitioner experience, not measurement.
Owner documentation for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, WebdriverIO, Testing Library and Android carries no publication date; it is cited as n.d. and treated as current at the access date.
Windows desktop UI automation: Microsoft's UI Automation AutomationId guidance bears on stable locators and is included; WinAppDriver's own docs were not searched separately.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.
